podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Distinguished as a Piano-Based "One Hit Wonder"
podcast.body: The New Radicals are widely recognized as a "one hit wonder" of the late 1990s, specifically noted as a piano-based act within the alt rock world. Their prominence stemmed from a single, successful piano-driven track from their album "Maybe You've Been Brainwashed Too." "this piano-based single became one of the great one hit wonders of the late 90s. Not just a one hit wonder from the alt rock world, but a piano-based, one hit wonder period."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Functioning as a Solo Project
podcast.body: The New Radicals operated more as a vehicle for Greg Alexander than a conventional band, with him being the only permanent member and Daniel Brisebois as a collaborator. This structure effectively made it Alexander's primary creative outlet. "band is a bit of a misnomer since he really was the only permanent member, along with a collaborator named Daniel Brizbois."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of The New Radicals as a Primary Vehicle
xref.body: In 1997, Greg Alexander formed The New Radicals, which operated more as a project for him than a traditional band, with Alexander as the only permanent member alongside collaborator Daniel Brisebois. This structure allowed him to be the principal creative force. "In 1997, he formed a band he called the new Radicals, and band is a bit of a misnomer since he really was the only permanent member, along with a collaborator named Daniel Brizbois."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Transition to Highly Sought-After Mainstream Songwriter
xref.body: Despite The New Radicals being known for a single major hit, Greg Alexander successfully leveraged that into a long-term career as a highly in-demand and well-paid mainstream songwriter. He has penned songs for numerous prominent artists, including Santana, Enrique Iglesias, Geri Halliwell, Rod Stewart, Kaiser Chiefs, and The Struts, sometimes using pseudonyms. "Well, that's because he's gone on to write songs for Santana and Enrique Glesias and Jerry Hallwell and Rod Stewart and Kaiser Chiefs and the Struts and many others, sometimes under his own name, sometimes under a pseudonym."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
